newsitem.title: USA: Chattanooga, Tenn., plans $40 mln sewer repairs.
newsitem.headline: Chattanooga, Tenn., plans $40 mln sewer repairs.

text.p: Chattanooga is proceeding with state-mandated sewer repairs that are expected to cost more than $40 million, a technician with the city's Department of Public Works said Thursday.
"We're working at it very strongly, we want to get it done by the deadline," technician Gordon Phillips said.
The Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation gave the city until July 1, 2000,to complete the repairs.
Mayor John Kinsey said the city had not decided whether to issue bonds to finance the work.
"We're going to wait and see what our needs are," Kinsey said.

Sewers in downtown Chattanooga were built in the early part of the century to carry both waste water and rain water. During heavy rains, the pipes are unable to handle the overflow and untreated waste is released into the Tennessee River and nearby creeks.
Under order from the Department of Environment and Conservation, the city is building storage areas to hold the overflow until the untreated water can be funneled to a treatment plant.
Chattanooga has already completed $6 million worth of repairs along the south bank of the Tennessee River.

Early this week, the City Council approved a $529,000 contract to build separation screens that will be used in a later phase of construction. Money for that portion of the project is already budgeted and comes from sewer user fees and property tax revenues, city spokesman Scott Wilson said.
